HERE IS YOOR CHALLENGE, 
0, COUNSELLOR! 


by Adele Ebbs, 

Director, Camp Wapomeo for Girls 
Taylor Statten Camps 


A shocker to me, if not to you, is 
that I have been camping for a little 
over fifty years, that’s half a century! 
During that time there have been 
changes, but there are many similarities 
in camping then and now, and in the 
opportunities and responsibilities await¬ 
ing the new counsellor. The more back¬ 
ground you can get for this job, the 
more you are going to feel “at home” 
with it. 

Let me reminisce a little, and per¬ 
haps this will stir memories for you 
loo, I remember my first portage 
(apparently a veiy short one) when 
I struck out ahead of my parents, then 
I went back to them, still with my pack 
on my back, to inform them the pack 
was too heavy — thus, in fact, cover¬ 
ing the portage twice! Only once did 
I have a fear of drowning, this while 
crossing an open bay in a high wind 
when I was middle man in the canoe. 
The only scar I carry is on one finger 
when I carelessly opened a can of sar¬ 
dines and part of my finger with it. 
The latter was stuck back on quickly 
and taped up by my smart counsellor. 

I remember: a family of otters sur- 
I’ounding our canoes at dusk once — 
hissing . . . , I remember when we 
found a heronry and one of the girls 


climbed a pine tree and got wonderful 
jYictures of those balls of fluff in their 
huge nest. I remember many beaver 
dams, which were a nuisance to lift 
our canoes and gear over, but which 
were of equal use to beavers and trip¬ 
pers, because we had water to paddle 
in. And there was the time we met a 
bear cub on a portage who just sat and 
stared, while we wondered uneasily 
where mama bear was. I remember 
being disturbed one night while sleep¬ 
ing in my bag under the stars — a 
persistent rustling just near my head— 
oh, it couldn’t have been anything but 
a mouse. I tried to ignore it, then took 
my flashlight from under my pillow 
and shone it into the eyes of a startled 
skunk—or, which of us do you think 
was the more startled? 

A counsellor is at heart a camper 

If you arc lucky enough to be able to 
get away from civilization, these things 
haven’t changed. But our “frontiers” 
are coming closer with their accessibility 


This article is based on the talk pre¬ 
sented by Mrs. Ebbs at the Ontario 
Camping Association Annual Confer¬ 
ence, March 1965. 


80 


Canadian Campino 



by road. You used to be able to bicycle 
out into the country for picnics; now 
you have to drive or go by bus to reacli 
the country. But there are good areas 
being saved by our Conservation Auth¬ 
orities. Nevertheless with recreational 
areas being made accessible, our 
country is opened up for tourism. This 
is an ever increasing challenge to cam¬ 
pers. We have to know and practise 
conservation. As counsellors we must 
cherish and share the thrill and excite¬ 
ment of our great out-of-doors, so that 
this won’t be lost to the next gener¬ 
ation. It is really no task to learn more 
about nature, so long as you continue 
to be curious about the unknown, alert 
to its magic, and you develop attitudes, 
interests and habits related to the wise 
use of resources. 

We want to be campers, and to me 
this means a fundamental desire to be 
in the out-of-doors: in the woods, on a 
high hill, by a lake or a creek, or in 
tlie sugar-bush of a friendly farmer. 
We don’t mind the weather—if it’s 
hot, we avoid the discomforts of sun¬ 
burn at the same time getting a healthy 
tan. If it’s wet and cold, we wear the 
proper gear and become more active. 
We kiiow there’ll be black flies the end 
of June and in early July, we know 
we’ll be pursued by mosquitoes and 
deer flies, so we dress for them and 
fight them! 

Your first season as a counsellor 

You are looking forward to being 
counsellors this summer. You are on 
the verge of becoming “the older gen¬ 
eration” in the eyes of your campers. 
But you arc all young enough to have 
the strength, the imagination, the 
N’ision, the courage, to give to your 
camps and campers leadership in pro¬ 
gramming and community living which 
can make this summer more exciting and 
worthwhile than any they have ever 
had. 


You can still remember your excite¬ 
ment at doing things for the first time: 
becoming water-borne with your first 
stroke as you learned to swim, paddling 
a canoe in a straight line, moulding 
a creation from some clay or carving 
it from a piece of wood, finding a bird’s 
nest and then going back regularly to 
peek and sec if the eggs had hatched. 
Discovering things for yourself for the 
first time is .so thrilling. Today’s “or¬ 
ganized” children need this release and 
lime for these explorations. Maybe you 
too have sulTcred from a highly or¬ 
ganized routine. Maybe this summer 
will be the first time when you can 
really do some thinking for yourself, 
so don’t crowd your programme or that 
of your campers. 

Do you understand the needs of 
your campers? 

There arc some needs so basic that 
you simply must remember them. To 
make it easier, memorize the code-word 
R.E.A.P.S., and the need represented 
by each letter. 

Recognition —In leaving the family 
circle, the camper needs to find 
his place in the camp family — he 
needs to have a part to play in the 
group, be it an activity group or his 
cabin group—and to get approval for 
acceptable behaviour. 

Experience (New) — adventure, 
excitement, time to explore—so let the 
camper have time to go fishing without 
a hook if he wants, time to watch the 
sun set or to catch a snake. 

Affection — and this isn’t just for 
little girls. We are too inclined to treat 
children as “little adults”. Don’t for¬ 
get that little boys need understanding 
and gentleness—they can’t always fight 
back and “be a man”. 


Toronto^ Canada, April 1965 


81 



Power — campers want to achieve^ 
but let it be at their level. Having put 
forth effort, they should then have 
some feelings of success and mastery. 

Security — realize what a sudden 
change it is for your campers from 
home to camp: new faces, and so many 
more people than at home, no city 
conveniences, sharing one’s “bedroom” 
with several others, strange night noises, 
different food, and so on. 

AH these children arc at different 
stages of development especially with 
relation to camp activities. Find out 
the level of ability of each one as soon 
as you can, and then help to make 
goals for each individual. 

The job of a counsellor is real work 

Some people make work out of play 
and some play out of work. We belong 
to the second category. We strive to 
create a holiday atmosphere, at the 
same time realizing the seriousness of 
our task. Counselling at camp this 
summer may be your first job. How 
lucky you are to work in a permissive 
and sympathetic atmosphere. Your 
camp director knows that you are 
serious in your desire to work, but 
also realizes that there must be some¬ 
thing more in it for you. Your edu¬ 
cation is continuing. This will be a 
growing-up experience because you will 
have to put your job first and your 
personal problems second. It will be 
harder to work with some than others, 
but you can’t always choose your cabin- 
mate or trip-mate, and so you will 
learn to get along with all kinds of 
people. 

There is dignity in having a job at a 
summer camp. More money can be 
made (and spent) waitressing at a 
lodge or doing highway contruction. 
But counselling has an important social 
meaning — you get the feeling that you 


are needed by others, that you arc play¬ 
ing an important role in the lives of 
others. You are not just a leader, you 
arc a counsellor, and in this you have 
an advantage over the camper’s parents 
in your opportunity to help him 
develop. 

Even in the South Seas where we 
say that no one has to work, this is 
really a fantasy because a woman there 
judges the worth of a man by, for ins¬ 
tance, his skill as a fisherman. 

You will be chosen for staff because 
of your individual attributes. Set your 
standards and goals and stick by them. 
Your contribution will be the greater 
if it is different from others on the 
staff. We are growing fortunate in 
Canada these days because we have 
young people not only from pioneer 
Canadian stock but also from other 
countries. If your cultural background 
is different, you can make a fine con¬ 
tribution by enriching various pro¬ 
grammes with stories, songs, dances 
and costumes. You have an important 
job which is going to influence eveiy 
child with whom you come in contact. 
It is wonderful to read about the in¬ 
fluence young people arc having abroad 
through C.U.S.O. and the Peace Corps. 
Tliis is for a very few, and no more 
important than the tremendous job to 
be done in our camps this summer. 

It takes many qualities and skills to 
make a good counsellor. It would be 
an asset to be a Master of Social Work 
or a trained psychologist, and perhaps 
as a l esult of your camping experience 
with children and people in general, 
you might enter one of these fields in 
your Iiigher education. In the mean¬ 
time you are not a “pro”, so when you 
lun into difficult situations, treat the 
indh'idual as a human being, show him 
you really care, and listen to his prob- 

page 110 please

lilhTH 

III the 

fuenijh nAiViriNU assijuiatidn 

(TAssocialion cles Caiiijjs du Quebec) 



by Tony Shor^an, 

Executive Secretary, 

Quebec Society for Crippled Children 


I am happy to have the oj^portimity 
ol outlining briefly how the French 
camps in this province formed into a 
group, which eventually resulted in 
thi‘ir becoming a part of the Quebec 
Camjhng Association, as I was privil- 
i‘ged in being able to do some ])ioneer- 
ing work in the fonnation of the French 
unit. 

As a member of the Canadian 
Camping A.s.sociation and the Quebec 
Camping Association, and also as 
Canijj Director of the Crippled Child- 
ren’s Camp, St. Alphonse, Joliette, 
Quebec, I attended a committee meet¬ 
ing in 1957 to pre])are for a coming 
joint Conference of the two Associa¬ 
tions. At that time, I iiK|uired if it 
would be possible to have a few sessions 
at such Conference in the French 
language, for the benefit of French- 
speaking Directors and stall' members 
of French camps. I felt this would 
be the first step towards the sharing of 
experiences and exchanging of \ icws by 
the French and English groups, for 
their mutual benefit. Some of the mem¬ 
bers were definitely against the prop¬ 
osition, others did not think French 
camp directors would be interested, 


and still others were in favour of it, 
jjro\ided sufFicient members joined. I 
asked for a few days’ delay to ascertain 
how many would be interested, and 
then contacted .several of my friends who 
were directors of French camps and 
told them of the plan being discu.ssed, 
asking if they wished to participate. 
Every member I called was enthusias¬ 
tic, and I arranged a meeting at my 
own office, with only 24 hours’ notice. 
Despite one of the worst blizzards we 
have ever had, there were some 18 
French-speaking Camp Directors at¬ 
tending. Miss Nan Vail, who is a 
Past President of the Quebec and Can¬ 
adian Camping Associations, also at¬ 
tended and both she and I explained 
tlie v arious aspects of the coming Con¬ 
ference and discussed the type of ses¬ 
sions we could have for French camps. 

Having been a member of the Que¬ 
bec Camping Association for fifteen 
years, I knew the value of having con¬ 
tacts with other Camp Directors, which 
the French camps did not have, and 
I am very j^roud and happy today to 
see the French and English groups 
vvwking together .so harmoniously, to 
their mutual advantage. An interesting 


Toronto, Canada, April IDGj 


83 



sideline is that one of the French- 
speaking members whom I canvassed 
in the early stages replied that he knew 
how to operate his camp and did not 
need anyone to dictate to him. My 
reply was that we did not need persons 
like him in the Association. This same 
gentleman later became President of 
the French section, which is an example 
of how our minds can be broadened 
by actually experiencing the advantages 
to be gained by the association of two 
groups differing widely in language and 
background. 

On April 12, 1958, at a meeting of 
the Canadian Camping Association and 
the Quebec Camping Association in the 
Windsor Hotel, a special session was 
conducted by a French-speaking gioup, 
to study the possibility of forming a 
French-Canadian section of the Assoc¬ 
iation. The suggestion was made to 
form a Committee for a year’s trial to 
learn more of the C.G.A.’s constitution. 
This idea was enthusiastically adopted, 
and I had the honor of being named 
President of the Committee which was 
immediately formed for this purpose. 
Many meetings were held, at one of 
wliich our group adopted the name 
“Association des Camps Canadiens 
Frangais. On July 17, 1958, at the 
Crippled Children’s Camp, St. Al- 
phonse, at a meeting under the honor¬ 
ary presidency of Monsignor J. A. 
Papineau, Bishop of Joliette, after 
much fruitful discussion, it was finally 
decided by all present to apply to have 
our Association become a part of the 
Quebec Camping Association. 

Election of officers of tlie now- 
permanent Association dcs Camps 
Canadiens Frangais took place on Nov¬ 
ember 15, 1958 when a full day’s study 
was held in the Mont St, Louis gym¬ 
nasium. I had the honor of being 
named President of the Association, and 
representatives were also elected for the 
Ottawa, Quebec and Montreal regions. 


In 1959, many activities were under¬ 
taken by our group, and a Newsletter 
was issued c\'ery two months; inter- 
camp visits were inaugurated, and it 
was most gratifying to hear of French- 
speaking camp directors vdsiting English 
or Jewish camps and being received 
most graciously and cordially, with all 
possible assistance and information 
being extended. 

It was decided, during 1960, to 
change the name of our group from 
“Association des Camps Canadiens- 
Fran^ais” to “Association des Camps 
du Quebec (Section Fran^aise)”, and 
it is a pleasure to report that as each 
year passes, more and more progress is 
achieved and the success of the group 
seems assured. 

I would like to take this opportunity 
of paying tribute to all the French- 
speaking and English-speaking Camp 
Directors, who, through their patience, 
co-operation and goodwill, have made 
possible the present status of French 
camps, which led to their merging with 
the Quebec Camping Association Inc. 
(English Section), as recounted by 
Mrs. Alta Kahn, President of the Pro¬ 
vincial Board of the Quebec Camping 
Association Inc.

WILD FLOWERS OF THE 
ROCKIES 

by George A, and Winifred V» Hardy 

Descriptions of 200 wild flowers are 
accompanied by 50 colour plates re¬ 
produced from original paintings 
which arc both accurate and beautiful 
by Frank L. Beebe. “The flora of the 
Rockies is unique for here we have the 
meeting place for 3 types of flowers: 
the moist western group, the dry eastern 
species, and the alpine.” From valley 
floor to mountain-top Mr. and Mrs. 
Hardy, both botanists from Victoria, 
B.C., gathered their material for this 
book, marvelling perhaps most at the 
enthralling wealth of bloom in the 
mountain meadows and alpland at or 
above timberlinc. Here, while the 
plants may be more dwarfed in stem 
and leaves, the flowers are often huge 
and profuse in colour and sheer wealth 
of bloom. Flowers which have turned to 
fruit in a valley, may be in bloom at 
timbcrline. 

The flow'crs arc grouped for easy 
identification in this book by colour 


and the family, botanical name, de.s- 
cription of flower, of leaves, its height, 
habitat are set out and then followed 
by information unique to the particular 
flower, this last being stated almost 
lyrically which gives one an idea of the 
pleasure the flower arouses in the 
observer. 

Frank L. Beebe is a naturalist and 
ornithologist as well as an artist with a 
fine talent for reproducing flowers on 
paper with accuracy and beauty. H, 
R. Larson Co., 11 McNab St. South, 
Hamilton; offices also in Saskatoon, 
and Vancouver.

RY 

IN 

Caap 



A Past President of Canadian Camping 
Association 

Founder of Canadian Camping Magazine 
Founder of Camp Glen Bernard 
Honorary Member^ Ontario Camping 
Association 


\ 

Poetry should have a place in the 
camp programme. It could be as im¬ 
portant as music, art or dramatics. 
However, unfortunately, prejudices 
hav'e to be overcome in introducing 
poetry to many young people today. It 
may be that they associate it with school 
home-work, or with modern poetry of 
the abstract variety which is too often 
difficult to understand. But imaginative 
leaders with a knowledge of our rich 
heritage of “singing verse” could make 
a programme of poetry a memorable 
experience in the life of a camper. 

It is probable that strategy may have 
to be used at first to introduce “Poetry 
evenings”. Perhaps it might help to 
have the impression get abroad that 
they are rather exclusive affairs. Plan 


a counter-attraction to lure away the 
more active people and to ensure that 
the poetry group is not too large. The 
circle will eventually widen as appre- 
would tell a story, making the action 
ciation grows. Make sure you reserve 
for the group a comfortable room: one 
with an attractive fire-place if possible, 
or a pleasant glade outdoors with per¬ 
haps a camp-fire glowing, if it is 
evening. 

Strateg)^ Ls also called for to produce 
the appropriate atmosphere—to create 
a subtle spell of enchantment. Nothing 
can work this magic more effectwely 
than a blazing wood fire, the soft glow 
of candle-light, and if possible, for 
added sorcery, an occasional handful of 
driftwood powder bursting into exotic 
blue-green flames. With the circle com¬ 
fortably grouped about the fire, the 
sound of rain or wind out of doors 
only adds to the pleasant sense of 
security and comradeship. 


86 


Canadian Camping 



It would be presumptuous to suggest 
to camp directors or counsellors the 
poems diey should read. We all have 
our favourites. It is most important, 
however, that any poems chosen should 
be read well. That means reading with 
a well-modulated voice and with dra¬ 
matic feeling. Read the poem as you 
come alive. With the music of words, 
you can awaken your listeners to all 
the beauty of the out-of-doors, the 
thrill of age-old adventures and the 
stirring emotions which, through the 
years, have dominated or inspired men 
and women. 

Perhaps one might be allowed to 
mention some of the poems which have 
been tried out successfully with campers. 
For the younger campers we suggest 
two collections—“Silver Pennies” and 
“More Silver Pennies” published by 
MacMillan Co. For older campers, 
there is a great wealth of dramatic 
poetry—such as the Indian legends of 
Pauline Johnson, Story pomes of Henry 
Van Dyke, including “Henry Hudson’s 
Last Voyage”, Alfred Noyes “The 
Highwayman”, excerpts from Long¬ 
fellow’s “Hiawatha”, the “Habitant 
Poems” of Henry Drummond, Wilson 
MacDonald’s “Song of the Ski”, ex¬ 
cerpts from E. G. Pratt’s poetry, Nature 
Poems like Van Dyke’s “God of the 
Open Air” and “Poems of Humour” 
by Edward Lear. The resources seem 
inexhaustible. 

In many camps a weekly Magazine 
or Scroll is produced by campers and 
counsellors to be read to the assembled 
group on a Saturday evening. This 
provides an opportunity for budding 
talent to produce original stories and 
verses. Though the poems may often 
be doggerel, there is occasionally a hint 
of latent genius, which, if given en¬ 
couragement, opens up a new avenue 
of expression. Even the effort to write 
a \erse often prompts a camper to sit 
down quietly and alone, to consider 


with “seeing eyes” the world about him. 
This experience in itself might be of 
greater value for an individual than 
any other experience camp can offer. 

A teen-age camper who later found 
her way into outstanding literary work 
in New York wrote one of her first 
poems at Camp. It illustrates the acute 
power of observation with which she 
watched a spectacular thunder storm 
and the poetic skill with which she 
described it for her camp friends. 


The Birches — to the Storm 

Yours is the victory, O splendid 
storm: 

Blow your triumphant bugles of 
the wind, 

Salute the world with lightning 
sword, and let 

Your tattered banners of the clouds 
stream out. 

We have no will, your glorious 
strides to check. 

Take your wild way with us: our 
branches bend 

Beneath your heavy silver lances’ 
thrust. 

We will not strike against your 
mighty lash 

Or match our light young limbs 
against your strength; 

But when you ha\'e gone by, when 
from the hill 

Sounds the last rumble of your 
chariot wheel. 

We shall remain, inviolate and 
calm,— 

Young gods with cloaks of green 
and slender make; 

The gay immortal dryads, we 
shall be 

The victors, by surrender, in 
the end.

HOW TO LEAD 


A NATURE HIKE 



by P. Af. Taschereau, Naturalist, 
Nova Scotia Museum of Science and 
Woodland Hoys^ Camp, Quebec 


Il7/y A ^^Natiire^^ Hike 

On a nature liike one conies to rec¬ 
ognize some of the coininon plants and 
animals, learn their habits and glimpse 
some of the complex relationships that 
exist between organisms and their en- 
\ ironment. In the course of a hike one 
can gain a familiarity widi native 
plants and animals that immeasurably 
increases one’s enjoyment of the out- 
of-doors. Ordinary hiking becomes 
more enjoyable when one recognizes 
familiar objects along the trail. 

This one actixity combines all the 
adxenture. of exploring, the excitement 
of discoxery and the fun of collecting. 
Observation, (‘ncouraged by the nature 


k'ader. shar|Jt‘ns the senses and in¬ 
creases the hik(‘r’s axvareness of the 
IxMiity and immense diversity of the 
lih* around him. 

I h*rc‘ is an ojipoi'tunity to encourage 
the inter(‘st of a child and open his 
i*yes to things really xvorth knoxving in 
the xvorld about him. Here is a chance 
to h(‘lp him to discern things as they 
rt'ally are and .see his place in a xvon- 
derful and orderly unixerse. 

To I'hr Leader 

hrom the bexvildering complexity and 
mass of nature, you. as leader, xvill have 
to sort out appealing details and inter¬ 
pret them to your listeners. 


88 


Canadian Camping 




An enthusiastic interest in nature, a 
desire to share this interest with others 
and some leadership ability are all that 
one needs to lead children on a nature 
hike. As your knowledge of nature 
grows and your appreciation of what in¬ 
terests people increases, so will your 
ability to lead a nature hike develop. 

When one becomes interested in a 
subject he soon learns something about 
it. As he develops knowledge of an 
interesting subject, his interest increases 
and there is a natural tendency to 
communicate this interest and enthus¬ 
iasm to others. 

Nurture your own nature interest by 
reading and gathering together into 
scrap books, suitable material from 
magazines, periodicals and newspapers, 
and by making collections of rocks, 
wildflowers, weeds, tree leaves and 
insects. 

Keep a notebook and in it record 
your own observations of nature, the 
names of newly discovered specimens, 
notes from reading correlated with your 
own findings, interesting facts about 
natural objects, evaluations of past 
hikes and what has interested your 
groups. 

“What is it?” or “What’s this called?” 
will become familiar questions to any¬ 
one who takes on the job of nature 
leaders as will the reply, “I don’t 
know,” to which should be added, 
“Let’s see if we can find out.” 

This “let’s learn together” attitude 
should be the approach for any leader 
not a specialist in his subject, and 
nature study is too broad a field for 
anyone to be a specialist in all its 
phases. 

Hiking and The Nature Hike 

A nature hike is a leisurely, obser¬ 
vant ramble, during the course of which 


things of interest are brought to the 
attention of the group by an experi¬ 
enced leader. 

In an ordinary hike the goal or 
destination must usually be reached 
within a certain period and thus hiking 
is not always leisurely with time for 
observation. 

The nature hike has a goal—some 
place to go with something to see or 
do—which gives it direction and pur¬ 
pose, but it may at times not attain its 
original goal because of something more 
interesting which is discovered along 
the way. 

Personal Preparation 

Go over, at least once, the area 
selected for the hike. Bring a note-book 
and pencil and take some inventoi'y of 
things of interest, noting objects or 
processes to be pointed out, and places 
for stopping. If possible get a botanist, 
geologist or other specialist to go along 
with you on these preliminary surv^eys. 

The leader should carry a knap-sack 
or collecting bag of the shoulder strap 
variety and preferably one with some 
division into pockets of various sizes. 
Several small empty boxes of pill-box 
size, a couple of killing tubes and a 
folded newspaper will be found most 
useful for holding specimens collected 
by the group. On his person, the 
leader will find it helpful to have a 
small hand lens, a sharp pocket knife 
and a note-book and pencil. 

Depending on the nature and direc¬ 
tion of the hike, a geological hammer, 
insect net, or binoculars can be carried 
by members of the group. Generally, 
these objects are eagerly sought after 
by the members of a young group and 
their use will require some supervision. 
They can, however, be of assistance in 


T or onto y Canada, April 1965 


89 



keeping the group together and holding 
their attention. 

Starting Out 

A group of twelve is about the limit 
for one leader to handle. On a nature 
hike, whether the group be large or 
small, there is generally a nucleus of 
about four or five enthusiasts who stay 
close to the leader and to whom most of 
the information is imparted. With larger 
groups, it will not be possible to keep 
all the individuals together. A more 
definite objective may be set — perhaps 
some questions to be answered, or a 
search for some plant or animal to be 
made along the way. 



Before starting off, seat the group in 
a semi-circle and explain what a nature 
hike is. Explain the direction and pur¬ 
pose of the hike, the necessity of stay¬ 
ing close to the leader, and mention 
some of the things one may expect to 
see (With city groups it may be neces¬ 
sary to put in a word about out-door 
manners—shutting gates, staying away 
front farmer’s buildings and cattle, dis¬ 
posing of refuse, etc.) 


"'Reseynble not the little snails 
That with their filth record their trails, 
Let it be known where you have been 
By leaving the woods and fields cleanT 

The first hike for new campers might 
be to explore the property and dis- 
co\ cr .something of the wildlife—birds, 
mammals, insects, plants and rocks and 
minerals that are to be found in the 
area. 

As the leader’s familiarity with the 
site increases and his knowledge of its 
areas of interest grows, other topics and 
hiking themes will suggest themselves: 
a hike up the shore to collect magnetic 
sand and clay concretions; a hike to 
the marsh to sec the ten foot tall 
Phragmites grass; a hike up the stream 
to where the beautiful jewel-like dog¬ 
bane beetles feed; a trip to the milk¬ 
weed patch to search for the elusive 
milkweed caterpillar. 

Something might be said at this time 
about “the earth beneath your feet,” 
the geological history of the area. How 
exciting it is to learn that the very 
ground you are standing upon was laid 
down long ago in vast inland seas, or 
forms part of the roots of ancient 
mountains more than one thousand 
million years old, or that only ten 
thousand years ago enormous fields of 
ice scratched and scoured this land, 
formed that distant hill and dropped 
these boulders we are resting upon. 
Many an interest in natural history has 
had its beginning in an enthusiasm for 
collecting rocks and minerals. 

During the course of the hike, things 
of interest are pointed out by the 


90 


Canadian Camping 



leader, questions answered and speci¬ 
mens identified. A nature hike for 
juniors is not the time for a lecture 
and unless there is a great deal of in¬ 
terest, lecturing enroute is not generally 
successful. Natiu'e games can be used 
on reaching the destination and before 
returning. 

Where To Look and What To 
Point Out 

Look under stones and fallen logs, 
beneath the bark of rotting trees, on 
the flowers of plants, under the eaves 
of buildings, in the pools along the 
shore, under flat rocks in running 
streams. Crack open the granite pebbles 
on the road to sec the clean un¬ 
weathered surface, and sweep the in¬ 
sect net through the gra.ss and shrub¬ 
bery along the roadside. 

Watch for galls, the local swellings 
of plant tissue, commonly caused by 
the workings of insects or mites. These, 
cut open with pocket knife, will often 
reveal their inhabitants. (Goldenrod 
sterns and the leaves of deciduous trees 
such as oak and poplar are good places 
to search for galls.) 

An appreciation of the continuous 
processes going on in the natural world 
is important to understanding the inter- 
I'elationships of living things. 

This may be seen in the work of a 
silt depositing stream which, along with 
wind, water and bir ds depositing seeds, 
changes what was once a swimming 
and boating area into a dense thicket 
of willow and sedge. 


It may be observed in the fonnation 
and filling of an ox-bow lake in a 
meandering creek, or the conversion 
of a fallen tree to soil. 

Following a break in the forest can¬ 
opy caused by the falling of a tree, 
a heavy cutting or fire, plants 
such as cherry, aspen, bramble and fire- 
weed sprout up. These plants, their 
seeds carried by the wind or in the 
feces of animals, move in and grow 
until replaced by other shade-tolerant 
species. 

Plant growth and the decay of dead 
plant tissues cause changes in soil 
humus and moisture and in the amount 
of light and nutrient available to other 
plants- Because of these changes, suc¬ 
cessively different plant communities 
will occupy a given territory in the 
course of time. This process, known as 
succession, is going on all around us 
and as a result our landscapes are 
continuously changing. 

In a bog, sphagnum mosses grad¬ 
ually fill in the edges and these are 



Toronto, Canada, April 1965 


91 


followed by sedges and acid soil heaths 
such as cranberry, blueberries, leather- 
leaf and lambkill. Eventually these may 
be succeeded by larch, spruce and fir. 

Examples of plant succession on rock 
may be encountered on nearly every 
hike. All stages of this interesting story 
can often be read on a single large 
rock. 

Beginning on bare rock, lichens can 
grow where no other plant could sur- 
\ ive. (The lichen plant is composed of 
two organisms, a fungus and an alga. 
The fungus prevents the alga from 
drying up and provides it with moisture 
and essential elements. The alga by 
means of sunlight conv^erts the water and 
mineral matter into food which it shares 
with the dependent fungus.) Growing 
only while moist, the lichens can re¬ 
main alive while dried up. Mineral salts 
are obtained in part from the rock and 
in part from rain water and wind¬ 
blown dust particles. When wet, the 
soft gelatinous body of the lichen ad¬ 
heres tightly to the rock. When dry, 
it contracts detaching minute fragments 
from the underlying surface. This 
mechanical action, supplemented by the 
chemical action of acids produced by 
the lichen, initiates soil formation. 

Decaying lichens and particles of 
rock form the first thin layer of soil 
and humus. On this layer other leafy 
lichens may succeed the first crust-like 
forms. Mosses able to withstand this 
dry environment come next. The mosses 
shade the lichens and compete with 
them for light, moisture and nutrients. 
.As the mosses grow, the older ones 


decay and add to the mat of humus 
which grows over the rock. Small ferns 
and grasses can take hold as this mat 
becomes thicker and develops a greater 
water-holding capacity. Eventually, as 
the soil layer increases, small shrubs 
and trees may take root. These shade 
the earlier plants which may then tend 
to disappear. 

In a forest climate the first trees may 
give way to other shade-tolerant trees 
which reproduce themselves, replacing 
individuals that die. Unless the climate 
changes or the community is disturbed 
by fire, man or other agencies, it will 
remain the same. 

Succession on bare rock does not 
always follow this sequence. If rock 
crevices and cracks arc filled with 
gravel or sand particles some of the 
earlier stages may be by-passed. 

The use of superlatives as examples 
will often catch interest — the oldest 
rock — the most poisonous plant — 
the largest bug — the most ferocious 
small mammal — the longest or short¬ 
est li\ ed, the rarest, or most common. 
Young animals of every kind from tad¬ 
poles and turtles to young mice turned 
up in a field, or insect larvae such as 
caterpillars, hav^e a special attraction. 
Some of these are easily kept for the 
camp period and may offer interesting 
oportunities for observing their trans¬ 
ition to adulthood. 

In answering questions, curiosity 
should be satisfied in such a manner 
that interest is aroused. When identi¬ 
fying a find, first question the group to 
see what knowledge they may have of

JAMAICAN 

FAREWELL 


byB, G. Lowes, 
Camp Timherlane 



Encouraged by the successes of 1963, 
the Ontario Camping Association, in 
partnership with the Canadian Uni¬ 
versity Students Ovei'seas Organization, 
raised almost $4000 again to bring ten 
young Jamaicans to Canada last sum¬ 
mer. Three young ladies and seven 
young men arrived at Toronto Inter¬ 
national Airport on June 20th to spend 
the next nine weeks in Ontario camps. 

The group was older, more mature, 
but no less excited about the prospect 
of spending the summer in Canada. 
After two days spent seeing Toronto 
and Niagara Falls, the guests were 
whisked off to camp by their hosts. 

In 1964, a number of camps 
“shared” trainees, one camp taking him 
for July and the other camp taking him 
over for August. This gav^e each trainee 
a much broader experience and also 
enabled twice as many camps and 
campers to have the adNantage of liv^- 
ing with our guests. 

Apart from almost perishing during 
our cool August, the Jamaicans enjoyed 
their stay and proved to be of value 
as counsellors. Most camps, in com¬ 


pleting an evaluation form felt that 
the guests had done an excellent or 
fine job. Their jobs varied from that 
of full counsellor, to floater and on 
down to C.I.T. 

Perhaps a number of quotations 
from camp evaluations will point out 
the host’s reactions most graphically: 

“It provided a practical demonstra¬ 
tion of non-discrimination.” 

“He brought a sensitivity for values 
often regarded lightly in North 
America.” 

“Mature interest and approach to 
the job. Conscientious.” 

“Sensitive to the feelings of the boys 
when teaching them.” 

“Infectious sense of humour.” 

“Very willing to try anything, a 
good example for the other staff.” 

“Sharing what life meant to a young 
person from a different country.” 

“Aware of present day issues.” 

“Silent example of racial equality.” 


94 


Canadian Camping 



There is no doubt that host camps 
and campers got more than they gave. 
The values to campers and staff were 
incalculable. The seeds of friendship 
and understanding planted and trans¬ 
planted should bear fruit and new seeds 
for many years to come. You cannot 
measure or weigh these values but you 
can certainly feel them. 

There were a few points of concern 
to those who studied the programme 
carefully: 

1. Half of the Jamaicans were not re¬ 
turning to Jamaica but were going 
abroad to study. 

2. The type of camping experience 
gained in Canada seems to have no 
relationship to camping as it is 
known in Jamaica, 


These two factors plus the fact that 
C.U.S.O. has decided to withdraw its 
financial support and redirect it, has 
lead the Board of O.C.A. to recom¬ 
mend that for 1965 the project be 
suspended. 

There was a recommendation that 
perhaps the energies could be re¬ 
directed towards an intra-Canadian ex¬ 
change^ across provincial boundaries in 
an effort to meld and weld the many 
peoples and interests into one. 

Surely, no one would disagree that 
communication, or lack of it, lies at the 
root of tlie world’s problems today. Any 
forms of exchanges and interchanges 
are like tiny candles lit in a dark 
cavern. If enough are lit by individ¬ 
uals, the darkness will be pushed back.

PRE-CAMP TRAINING 

IN THE SMALL CAMP 


by Helen Stewart^ Catnp Wahcahmie 

As presented at the Ontario Camping Association Conference, March 1965 


PRE PRE-CAMP PROCEDURE: 

1. Letters to “old’’ staff members re employment—sent in November 
or December. 

2. Prospective new staff members—application forms sent on request 

—reference forms on applicants mailed 
—interviews—at least one hour discussion 
—refusal or “sorry” letters to those not 
accepted. 

3. Letters of acceptance to staff members with contracts enclosed. 

4. In May, Staff Manual sent to eveiy staff member — contains a Job 
description, specific duties, etc. Some of the material is the same in all 
Manuals but additional data pertaining to a specific position is included 
—for example, canoeing counsellors, nurse, kitchen staff. 

5. Invitations sent in May to attend the June Mother and Daughter Week¬ 
end at camp—this week-end is a good orientation of camp. 

6. Letter in June with final instructions and suggestions. Pre-camp agenda 
sent then or included in Staff Manual. Letter stresses that pre-camp 
is a training course which means WORK. 

PRE-CAMP TRAINING: 

A. Reasons for having a pre-camp session: 

1. Orientation period —• necessary in order to have old and new staff 
personnel work together as a team so that when campers arrive staff is 
keen and ready for the summer ahead. 

2. Opportunity to review and learn (if necessaiy) skills and teaching 
techniques (especially valuable if no OCE or teacher training). 

3. “On the spot” discussion of our philosophy, procedures, regulations, job 
descriptions, schedules as outlined in the Staff Manual. 

4. All aspects of the programme covered by activity and discussion. 


96 


Canadian Camping 



5. Opportunity to check inventories and put equipment in readiness. 

B. Problems Involved: How Overcome 

1. Too expensive to waste It is stressed in June letter that her summer 

time—^is not an oppor- position is a vocation not a vacation—she 

tunity for staff to rest has accepted a job with a salary so she must 

and relax before camp arrive at camp with material ready for pre¬ 
opens. camp, and well-rested, fit to carry out her 

responsibility in pre-camp and the summer 
camping. 

2. To accomplish all that Pre-camp agenda — time is scheduled for 

must be covered in pre- activity periods, discussion sessions, practice 
camp, the staff must be of skills, free time, etc., through the 5-7 day 
kept on schedule. day pre-camp session. 

All actual labour in preparing camp com¬

Although we will miss the Quebec 
Camping Conference this year, we are 
pleased to note that plans for the 1966 
Conference have been in the making 
for quite some time. It is to be a bang- 
up affair we should all attend, in the 
Queen Elizabeth Hotel in Montreal; 
and we can report that the Queen E. 
is THE conference centre for our 
money. We look forward to a progress 
report as soon as the Executive can 
gi\c us an official release. 

CONGRATULATIONS 

... to a friend we made at last year’s 
Ontario Camping Association Confer¬ 
ence. Mr. Gibbs was our Guest Speaker 
at the Conference Banquet, his topic 
being Camping Imperatives for the 
Future (re-printed in Canadian Camp¬ 
ing, June, 1964). Now, a news release 
from the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion reads: 

“Howard G. Gibbs, of New York 
City, National Director of Programme 
Services for the Boys’ Clubs of Am¬ 
erica, has been named President-Elect 
of the American Camping Association. 

Mr. Gibbs is curi'ently a member of 
tlic National AG A Board of Directors, 
serving as Chairman of the ACA 
Standards Committee, a trustee of the 
ACA Foundation and Vice Chairman 
of the National Long-Range Study 
Committee. 

He is Cliairman of the Group Work 
Division of the National Association of 
Social Workers and was an official 
representati\’c of the Boys’ Clubs of 
.America to the White House Confer¬ 
ence on Children and Youth, at the At¬ 
torney General’s Conference on Juvenile 
Delinquency and to the United Nations. 
He is co-author of “Design for Juv¬ 
enile Decency.” 

After serving the coming year as 
President-Elect, Mr. Gibbs will be in¬ 
stalled as President at the National 
ACA Convention to be held in Chicago 
March 9-12, 1966.

The Montreal Mackay Centre for Deaf 
and Crippled Children’s Camp 

by P. M. McFarlane, 

Former Director 


“To the iiealtli and liappiness of 
physically dLsabled children of any race, 
colour or creed”. This dedication 
marked the official opening of the 
Camp on July 10, 1952. Members of 
the Board of Governors of the Center, 
civic dignitaries, some five hundred 
relatives and other guests participated 
in the ceremony. Thus came into being 
the realization of a dream of many 
Board members and friends that handi¬ 
capped children might enjoy camp life. 

Anyone who thinks that camp life is 
only for the able-bodied youngster 
should visit this camp. There are 
difTcrcnccs, of course, which set us apart 
from others, but the presence of wheel¬ 
chairs, crutches and braces does not 
interfere too greatly with a well-bal¬ 
anced activity programme designed to 
meet the needs and capabilities of the 
campers. Although there are similar 
camps across Canada, this one is unique 
in that the programme pattern which 
is followed attempts to duplicate as 
closely as possible that of a well- 
conducted private or institutional camp 
catering to normal children. Except 
for wooden ramps, which join roads 
and pathways to the various camp 
buildings, the physical features of this 
camp are quite similar to those of 
ordinary camps. The camp site itself 


testifies to this: located on Lake Massa- 
wippi, near Ayer’s ClifT, Quebec, the 
camp property, which covers twenty 
acres, has a natural sand beach, play¬ 
ground and ov^cr-night camping areas. 
The land itself is fairly hilly, a fact 
which caused some concern at the time 
of purchase. Nevertheless it was soon 
found that the children were able to 
move around quite well, and that meet¬ 
ing this extra challenge was advan¬ 
tageous to their development. 

The programme emphasis through 
the yca.rs has been based upon the 
assumption that it Is important that a 
physically disabled person be allowed 
to exprc.ss himself physically and men¬ 
tally in as normal a fashion as possible. 
Except for approximately forty boys 
and girls who participate in a scheduled 
physiotherapy and speech therapy pro¬ 
gramme, the campers take part in a 
very normal camp programme. Sched¬ 
ules for those taking therapy are 
arranged .so that these campers miss a 
minimum of camp activity. The cam¬ 
pers participate in a variety of activi¬ 
ties. These include swimming, over 
night camping trips, picnics, play days, 
fishing derbies, pony and boat rides, 
sing songs, interest groups—handicrafts, 
photography, nature study, dramatics, 
boating, fishing, art, ceramics, archery, 
athletics, astronomy, camp craft, wood 
craft, Indian lore—and cabin, sectional 
and “all camp” progi*ammcs. Wednes¬ 
day afternoon and evening is out-of 
camp picnic day. An all-camp pro¬ 
gramme is held every Saturday. This 



100 


Canadian Camping 




may be an “all-camper” birthday party, 
a square dance, a masquerade, a 
Christmas or New Year’s Party, an 
Indian Day, Midway, Circus, or Home¬ 
steader’s Day. 

There were several reasons why the 
Camp was established. Special therapy 
programmes which were having to be 
discontinued during the summer 
months could be carried on at Camp. 
The change of the scenery and activity 
for the children is a beneficial treat¬ 
ment in itself. The much needed rest 
thus received by the parents of the 
disabled children is also important. 
Crippling illness in a family can be a 
heavy strain on financial, physical and 
nervous resources. 

Because the Camp is an extension of 
the programme at the Center, it is 
financially dependent upon it for its 
major funds. Supplementary help has 
come to the Camp from various other 
sources. The Service Clubs of Montreal 
and Sherbrooke have been helped con¬ 
siderably. Except for the three initial 
buildings (2 large dormitories and a 
dining hall) all of the remaining facili¬ 
ties have been donated by groups or 
individuals interested in helping this 
very important work. These facilities 
include cabins, handicraft shop, audi¬ 
torium, library, administration building, 
boat house infirmary, physiotherapy 
and speech therapy buildings, ramps, 
boats, outboard motors, oars, waterfront 
docking etc. One of the most appre¬ 
ciated improvements made to the 
Camp was the paving of the roads 
and pathways in the immediate vicinity 
of the buildings and the waterfront. 
Level pathways and roads are a must 
in a camp where wheelchairs, braces 
and crutches are used for moving from 
one place to another. 

The camping season extends from 
the end of June to the middle of Aug¬ 
ust. About 90 percent of the children 
stay in camp for the entirc seven week 
period. Last summer, 145 boys and 
girls ranging in age from 16 to 19 


ycai's were enrolled. Most of these are 
pupils at the MacKay Center. Twelve 
campers were sponsored by the Sher¬ 
brooke Rotary and Kiwanis Clubs, and 
a small number of private sponsors. 

Very few adaptations are necessary 
in a camp of this nature except that a 
bit more floor space is required in the 
dining hall, cabins and the waterfront 
dock. Meals are served the same as in 
a normal camp. The rest hour periods 
arc at least one and one-half hours 
long. Generally, more sleep and 
rest is required in a camp of this 
nature. 

A large staff is required to do this 
specialized work. As well as the Exec¬ 
utive-Director of the Center in Mont¬ 
real, there is a Camp Director, 2 
Programme Directors, Handicraft and 
Waterfront Directors, Nursing Staff, 
Chef and his assistants. Laundress, Bus 
Driver, and a permanent Caretaker. 
The Counsellor-Camper ratio must be 
not less than 1-4. The Counsellors are 
all carefully chosen high school and 
university students. Three Physiothera¬ 
pists and a Speech Therapist are em¬ 
ployed full time. All staff personnel 
are jjaid a salary. It is amazing to 
realize the benefits the Counsellors gain 
from a summer spent here. This type 
of e.xpcrience enriches their liv^es and 
often channels their ambitions. After 
fourteen summers in operation, we note 
that many of our former Counsellors 
have become doctors, nurses, physio¬ 
therapists, social workers, or teachers 
of physically and mentally handicapped 
children. Some have recently become 
interested in Speech Therapy, the train¬ 
ing for which is just opening in 
Canada. 

As one can see, this Camp means 
many things to many people—the cam¬ 
pers, the parents, the staff. Through 
the years, every effort has been made 
to see that the dedication pledge of 
1952 has been followed with the cam¬ 
pers being the ones who have received 
the greatest benefit. —• 


Toronto, Canada, April 1965

THE PEACOCK CAMPING BOOK 

Rex Hazlewood and John Thunnan 

With out-trip camping and family 
camping dc\’cloping as it has, over the 
past few years, into a pastime requiring 
skill and imagination, a considerable 
amount of guidance by experts is 
desirable. Quite the best source of such 
guidance, outside of the official Boy 
Scout and Girl Guide handbooks, is a 
new publication from England, The 
Peacock Camping Book, As one of the 
Penguin series it is an easy size to slip 
into the pocket or knapsack. As a com¬ 
plete reference work, the authors have 
presented it in infinite detail for novice 
or hardened camper. The basics of 
whippings, knots and lashings, sanita¬ 
tion and hygiene, equipment, fires, axes, 
camp comfort, menus and cooking help 
to case the way and make each day 
and night happy and healthful. The 
last two chapters go into map-using 
and reading, as well as information on 
camping in Europe in an age when so 
many trips abroad are camping trips. 
A Peacock-Penguin Book — .85^. 

E.F.

Canadian Camping 




IDEAS 


by Margaret Govan, Camp Onawaw 


FOR INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMMES 


Campers are always interested in 
how ‘other’ people live, and as a result 
they throw themselves into any exper¬ 
ience which opens a window on 
another nationality, culture, or even 
the widely divergent grouping within a 
country like Canada. Such experiences 
can be very varied, and can suit almost 
any occasion. Resource material is so 
easily obtained. 

Many camps have Olympic days. 
These can be dressed up in all sorts of 
ways with flags, traditional ceremonies, 
etc. This is a natural, after all the 
T.V. coverage of last year. 

The Girl Guides ran a World’s Fair 
at Doe Lake last summer, and it seems 
a very timely project with the ‘Expo’ 
coming up. A preview would be in 
order. 

Festivals and Carnivals lend them¬ 
selves to camps. Floats can be made 
from boats, or stationary ones from 
booths. It is amazing how versatile 
and able camp groups are at producing 
ideas, working on costumes, and decor¬ 
ations, etc. A small committee is 
necessary to clear up the problems of 
duplication. Dancing, music, skits, and 
food can be incorporated into the total 
programme. 


On the smaller scale a meal from a 
country is always fun. (Campers find 
a tremendous interest in eating!) 
Almost any cook book can supply 
recipes, but spices and highly seasoned 
foods must be toned down to suit 
young tastes. Also some familiar food 
should be on the menu. Dressing up 
and decorations make such a meal a 
party. 

One or more countries can be the 
theme for a camp fire, and provides 
gi'eat scope. Or a party . . . our 
Jamaican counsellor was the resource 
material for a Caribbean party. (We 
had to censor the rum punch!) The 
Girl Guides had a Swiss mountain 
climbing expedition, and also a 
Japanese Tea House with a Kabuki 
theatre for afternon entertainment. 

The committee in charge will have 
to be aware of what is going on, for 
some of the campers’ impressions of 
other peoples are erroneous, and may 
lead to problems. Making other 
people’s customs a laughing matter is 
usually pure ignorance and in poor 
taste.

SiMIHAR 


by Dr. Medley Dimock, 

Sir Geor<ie W illiams University 

Montreal, Quebec V 


“Boy, you really have lo woik at it 
lo make democracy function”. 

So remark(‘(l one of the campers at 
a residential training jnogramme in 
inter-cultural r(‘lations wliich took place 
at (loldeye Lake Clamp in Alheita and 
was sponsoi(*d hy the Farm Womens 
Union of Alberta. Twenty-five yoiitLs 
participat(‘d; eleven were Indians, two 
were Eskimos and twelve were dele¬ 
gates from farm unions. The ages 
ranged from fourteen to twenty-one, 
with a median of eighteen. Eleven 
were hoys and fourteen were girls. Most 
had completed grade nine. An attempt 
had be(‘n made to have even more 
Indian repre.sentatives in order to make 
sure the Indians had ecjual status. In¬ 
dians were in\ ited to participate on the 
stafL but this did not work out, so 
that the stall’ rej^resented the non- 
Indian group. 

In an efVort to implement the 
assumption that “Education is a co- 
operatixe j)rocess involving the learners 
and that they should participate in 
planning the |)rogramme and other 
decisions which alTect them”, the stall 
met before camp and made as few 
d(‘cisions as possible in order to leave 
as large an ar(‘a as ])ractical within 


which the cam|K*rs could make de¬ 
cisions. The goals of the project were 
defined as “Sharing our heritage, de- 
\ eloping a better understanding among 
Indians and non-Indians, and increas¬ 
ing the citizenshij^ and leadership cap¬ 
acity and responsibilities of all.” The 
training design attempted to work to¬ 
wards these goals by developing a 
miniature community founded on 
d('mocratic procedures where all could 
work together towards connnon goals. 
Maximum freedom was allowed the 
youths lo plan, o]X'ratc and evaluate 
their own j^rogramme. 

Tin* stair helped to establish a 
climate of .security and trust where 
there was freedom for all to express 
tluanselves and try out new behaviour. 
In order to be equal members of the 
community, stall were to play down 
their status and participate fully in 
community activities. Their resources. 
])lus the resources of the camp site and 
its social and recreational facilities, 
would be available to all. In their role 
of community members, staff would also 
model giving “feedl^ack”, or reactions, 
to behaviour or events and hel]D to set 
a standard of all evaluating their ])ro- 
gress towards the goals for the ]Dro- 


104 


Canadian Camping 



gramme. Within the limits of the camp 
operation (meals, lights out, water 
safety, etc.), all programmes would be 
allowed to develop from within the 
community and the stafF, other than 
stated above, would not attempt to in¬ 
fluence programme towards their needs 
or their personal objectives. 

Notes and Observations 
ON THE Programme 

The campers arrived in the evening 
and the ne.xt morning the total group 
gathered to consider how they could 
set up an organization or structure that 
could plan and carry out the things 
they wanted to do during the week. 
This session was introduced with a des¬ 
cription of the learning goals and pro¬ 
cedures that would be used to work 
towards the objectives of the seminar. 
From here on the staff attempted to 
facilitate the development of an opera¬ 
tional structure by gradually turning 
the responsibility over to the total 
group. 

After considering several possible 
structures, a compromise developed 
that divided the total community into 
five groups. Each group was to select 
a member to represent them on a com¬ 
munity co-ordinating council and this 
council was to elect a chairman from 
among their five members. Then the 
fi\ e groups were to rotate, each of the 
fi\ e days, on the programme and com¬ 
munity needs (recreation, educational 
sessions, entertainment, canteen and 
kitchen duties). The adults were to 
become part of this operation and not 
act as advisers to the various groups. 

The next question was how to form 
into the five small groups. Some par¬ 
ticipants were ready to count off by 
five, but after further consideration it 
^vas agreed to make up the groups on 
a heterogeneous basis considering age, 
sex, race and interests. By mid-afternoon 


the community council was formed and 
the other groups were meeting. The 
council decided to have two educa¬ 
tional periods each day, one would be 
tlie responsibility of each group on a 
rotational basis and the other would be 
turned over to the adults. 

The adults (as they were no longer 
referred to as staff) met to jilan their 
educational programmes and it was 
decided to use a continuing small group 
method. These groups meeting for two 
hours each morning would focus on 
interpersonal relations and social sensi¬ 
tivity. Members would be encouraged 
to share their previous experience in 
inter-group relations and ix^spond to the 
experiences of other members. 

Many of the campers found the 
initial planning stage long and frustrat¬ 
ing. Their expectation had been that 
the staff would set up the programme 
and tell them what to do. In planning 
it themselve.s, and for most this was 
their first such experience, they found 
it took much longer and there were 
more aspects to consider and discuss 
than they had imagined. 

For the remainder of the week the 
programme operated almost as planned. 
The council had to meet twice or more 
each day to keep up with new situations 
and to keep the other groups co-ordin¬ 
ated, The council did not provide an 
opportunity for its representatives to 
meet with their groups for any further 
briefing or checking of point of view. 
Hence, some of the problems were cre¬ 
ated by this lack of communication of 
the council with the total camp 
community. 

The small educational groups pro¬ 
vided considerable continuity to the 
programme. As these groups developed 
and members came to trust one an¬ 
other, they were able to share real feel¬ 
ings about individual differences. At

STARKMAN CHEMISTS

WA. 2 - Twenty-One - Twenty-One 


first everyone said Indians, or a min¬ 
ority group, were just the same as 
everyone else and there was no dis¬ 
crimination or problem. The Indians 
also said they felt just the same as 
others and had not encountered any 
problems through being an Indian. 
Later they started to reveal some of the 
concerns that they had, described some 
of the difficult situations they had been 
in, and finally discussed their relations 
in the present group. 



The recreational and social pro¬ 
gramme showed a return to the tra¬ 
ditional way of doing things and 
jjrovided a great deal of security for all. 
Everyone participated in the recreation 
and at some points the adults had 
difficulty in not dominating the activi¬ 
ties. An adult with physical and social 
skills can find it difficult to see a game 
of volleyball being played without an 
umpire and the net sagging six inches 
in the middle. To give up control of 
a camp programme is not an easy thing 
and requires both an understanding of 
the educational objectives and method 
as well as patience and personal 
security. 

This relutcance to give up control 
became most apparent when things 
deviated from normal or something 
happened which was against adult ex¬ 
pectations. There were several inci¬ 
dents of this nature during the camping 
programme and sometimes the staff 
would step in and deal with them as 
authority figures rather than allowing 
them to be worked out within the total 


106 


Canadian Camping 




camp. Certainly, it is easier to share 
control and decision-making when 
things are running smoothly and ac¬ 
cording to adult expectations. The real 
test of democratic procedures is that 
their functioning is supported in all 
types of situations. 

The major intercultural dimension 
that evolved during the week was the 
identification and acceptance of indi- 
\'idual differences along with an oppor¬ 
tunity for the community to become 
aware of the resources within its mem¬ 
bers and to utilize these resources. The 
two Eskimo girls helped with the identi¬ 
fication and acceptance of individual 
differences of race and culture as they 
were quite ready to talk about what it 
was like to be an Eskimo, and some of 
the inter-group problems associated 
with rapid social change that they en¬ 
countered in moving into a “modern” 
society. This helped the Indians to 
own their differences and share some of 
their heritage. This was typified by a 
demonstration of Indian dances on the 
final evening. The owning and recog¬ 
nition of differences spread to looking 
at farm and urban living, differences in 
age and sex, and the practices of differ¬ 
ent religions. 

It is likely, too, that most of the 
activities during the week provided 
opportunity to interact around goals 
that were real and desired by all. The 
exceptions were a few traditions that 
had been inherited from the regular 
camp programme. In any case, a large 
percentage of the programme origin¬ 
ated within the community and was 
carried out by the community. This is 
best described as a developmental pro¬ 
gramme in which the adults joined the 
community and continued to share their 
resources which might build a more fully 
functioning community where individ¬ 
ual differences and resources would be 
recognized and used to the benefit of 
all. ^

(b) Inventories checked and equipment readied in ail activities for camp 
use—^placed on waterfront and at each activity site. 

(c) Bulletin Boards—progress charts drawn up by activity counsellors and 
posted on bulletin boards, placed at each activity site—also posted are 
the activity tests. 

(d) Lesson plans—for every activity for 1 week submitted to Head of 
Waterfront or Head of Programme (where applicable)—checked and 
returned. Same procedure followed through summer. Activity counsel¬ 
lors are teachers with no teacher training, usually. Lesson plans help 
them to organize their material and produce the best possible. Staff 
members request and desire this practice. 

(e) Time for recreation and rest—swimming, volleyball game, waterpolo, 
campfires and sing-songs, waterskiing. At end of day, food ’n relaxation!

evening

THE GREB HIKING BUREAU 
was formed last year as a public service 
with two purposes in mind: to inform 
people of hiking as a sport and 
recreation; and to acquaint them with 
trails and the unlimited opportunities 
for hiking which Canada presents. We 
have received the following communi¬ 
cation from THE GREB HIKING 
BUREAU, 1 Adam St., Kitchener, 
Ont. 



research 


become 


MODEKN, 

FAST, ECONOMICAL 

METHOD of controlling 
those pesky Mosquitoes 
and Black Flies 


obvious that the two major obstacles 
to the more widespread acceptance 
of hiking among Canadians is lack of 
information about hiking trails, and, 
of course, the shortage of trails. 

A preliminary booklet, “Hiking 
Trails in Canada” should help to over¬ 
come the first problem. The Bureau 
has published this in preliminary form 
so that you with special interests in 
the outdoors may have an opportunity 
to study the contents before the first 
edition is printed. We hope you will 
regard this booklet as important 
enough to warrant your critical assess¬ 
ment and that you will pass your com¬ 
ments and criticisms on to us. 

As far as we know, this is the first 
compilation of hiking trails in Canada, 
and it is by no means an exhaustive 
list. However, if you know of any 
trails that have been omitted, or any 
that are incorrectly listed, we would 
appreciate hearing from you. Your 
co-operation in this will be another 
contribution towards helping Cana¬ 
dians to enjoy the outdoors. 

Yours very truly, 

Charles E. Greb, Director”

IDEAS 


Resource materials need to be at 
camp, and the crafts department 
aware that it may have to help provide 
costumes, decorations, etc. But the 
final decisions as to the programme 
should be made at camp. No pro¬ 
gramme director must set his heart on 
doing this or that some time in mid¬ 
winter. Such a festival loses all 
spontaneity and becomes an adult 
decision. 

Suggested Reference Books: 

Children’s Festivals from Many 
Lands, Millen, Friendship Press. 
Unicef Materials.

Harkin. 

Bible Qui:^—Wells & Davis. 

Book of American Indian Games—

O, COUNSELLOR 


Icms. So much can be accomplished by 
talking things out to a sympathetic 
listener. You too will find opportunities 
to talk with your colleagues and super¬ 
visors, and do some personal planning 
for the future. If you can be receptive 
to others — reach out — share — give 
of yourself — this is what will make 
for a successful summer. And when 
you sit down to evaluate it, you will 
find that mutual sympathy and gener¬ 
osity of spirit make up the secret of 
true happiness. 

The counsellor’s job is a demanding 
one. It can’t be taken lightly, but the 
rewards are there. You’ll see them in 
the smiling face of a camper, the com¬ 
radeship of your fellow stafT, and the 
warm handshake of your camp director 
which will mean “Thanks. Well done!”
